screens.title: Layer 4 vs. Layer 7 Load Balancing
screens.narratorSegment: Let's start by clarifying a crucial distinction in Azure's load balancing services: Layer 4 versus Layer 7. Azure Load Balancer operates at Layer 4, the Transport Layer, of the OSI model. This means it makes routing decisions based purely on IP addresses and port numbers. It's excellent for distributing network traffic across virtual machines or services, regardless of the application protocol. Think of it as a high-speed traffic cop directing vehicles based on their destination address and lane. In contrast, Azure Application Gateway is a Layer 7 load balancer, operating at the Application Layer. This allows it to inspect the actual content of an HTTP or HTTPS request, such as the URL path or host headers. This deeper understanding of the application protocol enables more intelligent routing decisions, making it ideal for web applications. For example, it can route requests for '/images' to an image server farm and '/api' to an A P I backend. This fundamental difference dictates when and where each service should be used, with Application Gateway offering specialized features tailored for web application delivery and security.

content.html:
Module 05›Chapter 5.7›Layer 4 vs. Layer 7 Load Balancing
Core Concept

Layer 4 vs. Layer 7 Load Balancing

Understanding the fundamental difference between Azure Load Balancer and Application Gateway

Key Differences

  • •
    Operating Layer: Load Balancer at Layer 4 (Transport); Application Gateway at Layer 7 (Application).
  • •
    Routing Logic: Load Balancer uses IP/Port; Application Gateway uses URL path, host headers, etc.
  • •
    Primary Use: Load Balancer for general network traffic; Application Gateway for web applications.
  • •
    Advanced Features: Application Gateway offers SSL offloading, WAF, URL routing, multi-site hosting.
Key Takeaway

Choose Azure Load Balancer for basic TCP/UDP traffic distribution and Azure Application Gateway for advanced web application traffic management.

Common Misconception

Assuming all load balancers are interchangeable. Their operating layer dictates their capabilities and ideal use cases.

Load Balancer vs. Application Gateway

Azure Load BalancerLayer 4 (Transport)
  • TCP/UDP traffic
  • IP address & port based
  • High performance, low latency
Application GatewayLayer 7 (Application)
  • HTTP/HTTPS traffic
  • URL path & host header based
  • Advanced web features

Example Scenario

For a simple backend database cluster, use a Load Balancer. For a public-facing e-commerce site needing WAF and SSL, use an Application Gateway.

screens.title: Key Features of Application Gateway
screens.narratorSegment: Azure Application Gateway comes packed with a suite of advanced features specifically designed to optimize and secure web applications. These capabilities go far beyond basic traffic distribution. For instance, it offers SSL/TLS Termination, which offloads the computationally intensive task of decrypting HTTPS traffic from your backend servers, allowing them to focus on serving content. The integrated Web Application Firewall, or WAF, provides robust protection against common web vulnerabilities like S Q L injection and cross-site scripting, acting as a crucial first line of defense. Furthermore, Application Gateway enables intelligent traffic routing based on the actual content of the HTTP request. This includes URL-based routing, where requests to different paths can be directed to distinct backend server pools, and Multi-site Hosting, which allows a single Application Gateway to serve multiple domain names. It also supports Session Affinity, ensuring a user's requests consistently go to the same backend server, which is vital for stateful applications. These features collectively make Application Gateway an indispensable tool for modern web application architectures. screens.title: SSL/TLS Termination (Offloading)
screens.narratorSegment: One of the most valuable features of Azure Application Gateway is SSL/TLS Termination, often referred to as SSL Offloading. When a client connects to your web application over HTTPS, the Application Gateway can handle the initial decryption of that SSL/TLS traffic. This means that your backend web servers, which actually host the application, receive unencrypted HTTP traffic. The primary benefit here is a significant reduction in processing overhead on your backend servers. SSL/TLS encryption and decryption are computationally intensive tasks, and offloading them to the Application Gateway frees up your backend resources to focus solely on serving application content, thereby improving overall performance and scalability. Furthermore, it simplifies the configuration of your backend servers, as they no longer need to manage SSL certificates or handle encryption. Application Gateway can also re-encrypt the traffic before sending it to the backend for end-to-end encryption, ensuring data remains secure even within your private network. This flexibility allows you to balance security and performance effectively. SSL/TLS Termination (Offloading) means ssl/tls termination offloads decryption from backend servers, boosting performance and simplifying their configuration, with optional re-encryption for end-to-end security.. In practical terms, understanding how application gateway handles encryption and decryption for web traffic. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Module 05›Chapter 5.7›SSL/TLS Termination (Offloading)
Deep Dive

SSL/TLS Termination (Offloading)

Understanding how Application Gateway handles encryption and decryption for web traffic

How it Works

  • •
    Client Connection: HTTPS traffic arrives at Application Gateway.
  • •
    Decryption: Application Gateway uses its installed SSL certificate to decrypt the traffic.
  • •
    Backend Forwarding: Traffic is forwarded as unencrypted HTTP to backend servers.
  • •
    Optional Re-encryption: Application Gateway can re-encrypt traffic to backend for end-to-end security.
Key Takeaway

SSL/TLS termination centralizes certificate management and reduces backend server load, improving application performance.

Pro-Tip

Always ensure your SSL certificates are correctly configured and renewed regularly for HTTPS listeners to avoid service interruptions.

SSL/TLS Offloading Process

Client (HTTPS)
Application GatewayDecrypts HTTPS
Backend Servers (HTTP)

Example Use Case

An e-commerce site uses SSL termination to offload encryption from its web servers, allowing them to handle more customer requests efficiently.

screens.title: Web Application Firewall (WAF)
screens.narratorSegment: Security is paramount for any web application, and Azure Application Gateway's integrated Web Application Firewall, or WAF, provides a critical layer of defense. WAF protects your web applications from common web vulnerabilities and exploits, such as S Q L injection, cross-site scripting, and other threats identified by the OWASP Top 10. It does this by inspecting incoming HTTP/HTTPS traffic and applying a set of rules to detect and block malicious requests before they reach your backend servers. WAF can operate in two modes: detection mode, where it logs threats without blocking them, which is useful for initial testing and tuning; and prevention mode, where it actively blocks detected threats, which is the recommended mode for production environments. Implementing WAF centralizes your web application security, reducing the burden on individual backend servers and providing a consistent security posture across your application landscape. It's a powerful tool to safeguard your applications against a wide range of cyberattacks, ensuring data integrity and service availability. screens.title: URL-based Routing & Multi-site Hosting
screens.narratorSegment: Azure Application Gateway's Layer 7 capabilities truly shine with features like URL-based routing and multi-site hosting. URL-based routing allows you to inspect the URL path of an incoming request and direct it to a specific backend pool. For example, if your application serves images from slash images slash asterisk and videos from slash video slash asterisk, you can configure the Application Gateway to send requests matching slash images slash asterisk to a backend pool optimized for image delivery, and slash video slash asterisk requests to a video streaming backend. This provides granular control over traffic distribution and allows for specialized backend services. Multi-site hosting takes this a step further by enabling you to host multiple distinct web applications on a single Application Gateway instance. It achieves this by examining the host header in the HTTP request. So, requests for site1. com can be routed to one set of backend servers, while requests for site2. com are sent to another, completely separate backend. This is incredibly cost-effective and simplifies management for organizations hosting multiple web properties. Both features leverage the Application Gateway's deep understanding of HTTP to provide flexible and efficient traffic management.

Routing Logic

URL-based Routing & Multi-site Hosting

Directing traffic based on URL paths and hosting multiple applications on one gateway

How They Work

  • •
    URL-based Routing: Routes requests to different backend pools based on the URL path (e.g., /images/*).
  • •
    Multi-site Hosting: Routes requests to different backend pools based on the HTTP host header (e.g., site1.com vs. site2.com).
  • •
    Efficiency: Consolidates multiple applications or services behind a single Application Gateway instance.
Key Takeaway

These features provide granular control over web traffic, enabling flexible application architectures and cost-effective hosting.

Common Mistake

Incorrectly configuring host headers on backend web servers for multi-site setups, leading to routing failures.

screens.title: Application Gateway Components
screens.narratorSegment: To effectively deploy and manage an Azure Application Gateway, it's essential to understand its core architectural components. First, we have the Frontend IP configuration, which is the public or private IP address where clients connect to the gateway. Next are Listeners, which define the IP address, port, and protocol—HTTP or HTTPS—for incoming client requests. Listeners are also responsible for handling SSL certificates for termination. Request routing rules are the heart of the gateway's intelligence; they link a listener to a backend pool and specify how requests matching the listener are routed, enabling URL-based routing and multi-site logic. Backend HTTP settings define parameters for how the Application Gateway connects to the backend servers, such as port, protocol, cookie-based affinity, and connection draining. Backend pools are groups of servers—VMs, VM scale sets, App Services, or external IPs—that host your web application. Finally, Health probes continuously monitor the health of these backend instances, ensuring traffic is only sent to healthy servers. These components work in concert to provide a robust and flexible web application delivery system. screens.title: Deploying Application Gateway: Subnet Requirements
screens.narratorSegment: Before you can deploy an Azure Application Gateway, it's crucial to understand its networking requirements, particularly regarding subnets. Application Gateway requires a dedicated subnet within your virtual network. This means that no other resources, such as virtual machines or other Azure services, should reside in the same subnet as your Application Gateway instances. This isolation ensures optimal performance and security for the gateway. The subnet size is also important; it must be large enough to accommodate the number of Application Gateway instances you plan to deploy, including any scaling needs. While there's no specific name requirement for this subnet, a slash 24 or slash 27 address prefix is commonly used, providing enough IP addresses for typical deployments. For example, a slash 27 subnet provides 32 IP addresses, of which 5 are reserved by Azure, leaving 27 usable IPs. This is usually sufficient for a standard Application Gateway deployment with scaling. Step 3: Create Application Gateway

az network application-gateway create \
  --resource-group NetworkingLabRG \

screens.title: Deploying Application Gateway: Backend Pool & Common Mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: After creating the Application Gateway, the next critical step is to define its backend pool targets. A backend pool is essentially a collection of servers that host your web application. These can be virtual machines, virtual machine scale sets, Azure App Services, or even external IP addresses. We'll use the az network application-gateway address-pool update command to add our Nginx VMs to the default backend pool. It's important to correctly identify the network interface card, or NIC, IDs of your backend servers to ensure they are properly registered with the gateway. Once added, the Application Gateway can begin distributing traffic to these instances based on your routing rules. However, it's equally important to be aware of common mistakes. Not providing a dedicated subnet, as discussed earlier, is a frequent issue. Misconfiguring health probes is another, especially for complex applications where the default probe path might not accurately reflect application health. Finally, incorrect URL path rules or host headers for multi-site setups can lead to traffic not reaching the intended backend. Careful attention to these details ensures a robust and functional Application Gateway deployment.

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome to this chapter on implementing Azure Application Gateway. In today's digital landscape, web applications are at the heart of many businesses, and ensuring their performance, security, and scalability is paramount. Azure Application Gateway is a powerful service designed specifically for this purpose. Unlike traditional load balancers that operate at a lower network layer, Application Gateway understands the intricacies of web traffic, allowing it to make intelligent routing decisions based on the content of HTTP requests. This capability unlocks advanced features like protecting against common web vulnerabilities, offloading SSL encryption, and directing traffic based on URL paths. By the end of this chapter, you'll have a solid understanding of how to leverage Application Gateway to enhance your web application deployments on Azure, making them more robust and secure. Let's dive into how this essential service can transform your application delivery.

In this chapter, we'll focus on several key learning objectives that will equip you with practical skills for managing web traffic in Azure. Our first goal is to clearly differentiate between Azure Load Balancer and Azure Application Gateway. While both distribute traffic, they operate at different network layers and offer distinct capabilities. Understanding when to use each is crucial for designing efficient and resilient architectures. We'll explore their respective use cases, helping you make informed decisions for your deployments. For instance, if you need simple, high-performance distribution of TCP/UDP traffic, a Load Balancer might suffice. However, if your web application requires advanced features like SSL offloading or URL-based routing, Application Gateway becomes the clear choice. This foundational understanding will set the stage for mastering the more advanced features of Application Gateway.

Continuing our journey, our third objective is to equip you with the practical skills to deploy and configure an Azure Application Gateway. This involves understanding and setting up its core components: listeners, rules, and backend pools. We'll walk through the steps necessary to bring an Application Gateway online, ensuring it's ready to manage your web traffic effectively. This hands-on knowledge is critical for anyone looking to implement robust web solutions in Azure. Finally, we'll delve into implementing advanced routing scenarios, specifically URL-based routing and multi-site hosting. These features allow you to direct traffic to different backend services based on the URL path or host headers, enabling you to host multiple applications efficiently on a single Application Gateway instance. We'll also integrate Web Application Firewall, or WAF, for enhanced security, protecting your applications from common web vulnerabilities. Mastering these configurations will enable you to build highly flexible and secure web application delivery systems.

Let's start by clarifying a crucial distinction in Azure's load balancing services: Layer 4 versus Layer 7. Azure Load Balancer operates at Layer 4, the Transport Layer, of the OSI model. This means it makes routing decisions based purely on IP addresses and port numbers. It's excellent for distributing network traffic across virtual machines or services, regardless of the application protocol. Think of it as a high-speed traffic cop directing vehicles based on their destination address and lane. In contrast, Azure Application Gateway is a Layer 7 load balancer, operating at the Application Layer. This allows it to inspect the actual content of an HTTP or HTTPS request, such as the URL path or host headers. This deeper understanding of the application protocol enables more intelligent routing decisions, making it ideal for web applications. For example, it can route requests for '/images' to an image server farm and '/api' to an A P I backend. This fundamental difference dictates when and where each service should be used, with Application Gateway offering specialized features tailored for web application delivery and security.

Azure Application Gateway comes packed with a suite of advanced features specifically designed to optimize and secure web applications. These capabilities go far beyond basic traffic distribution. For instance, it offers SSL/TLS Termination, which offloads the computationally intensive task of decrypting HTTPS traffic from your backend servers, allowing them to focus on serving content. The integrated Web Application Firewall, or WAF, provides robust protection against common web vulnerabilities like S Q L injection and cross-site scripting, acting as a crucial first line of defense. Furthermore, Application Gateway enables intelligent traffic routing based on the actual content of the HTTP request. This includes URL-based routing, where requests to different paths can be directed to distinct backend server pools, and Multi-site Hosting, which allows a single Application Gateway to serve multiple domain names. It also supports Session Affinity, ensuring a user's requests consistently go to the same backend server, which is vital for stateful applications. These features collectively make Application Gateway an indispensable tool for modern web application architectures. Key Features of Application Gateway means application gateway provides ssl offloading, waf, url-based routing, multi-site hosting, and session affinity for robust web app management.. In practical terms, exploring the advanced capabilities that enhance web application delivery. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

One of the most valuable features of Azure Application Gateway is SSL/TLS Termination, often referred to as SSL Offloading. When a client connects to your web application over HTTPS, the Application Gateway can handle the initial decryption of that SSL/TLS traffic. This means that your backend web servers, which actually host the application, receive unencrypted HTTP traffic. The primary benefit here is a significant reduction in processing overhead on your backend servers. SSL/TLS encryption and decryption are computationally intensive tasks, and offloading them to the Application Gateway frees up your backend resources to focus solely on serving application content, thereby improving overall performance and scalability. Furthermore, it simplifies the configuration of your backend servers, as they no longer need to manage SSL certificates or handle encryption. Application Gateway can also re-encrypt the traffic before sending it to the backend for end-to-end encryption, ensuring data remains secure even within your private network. This flexibility allows you to balance security and performance effectively. SSL/TLS Termination (Offloading) means ssl/tls termination offloads decryption from backend servers, boosting performance and simplifying their configuration, with optional re-encryption for end-to-end security.. In practical terms, understanding how application gateway handles encryption and decryption for web traffic. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Security is paramount for any web application, and Azure Application Gateway's integrated Web Application Firewall, or WAF, provides a critical layer of defense. WAF protects your web applications from common web vulnerabilities and exploits, such as S Q L injection, cross-site scripting, and other threats identified by the OWASP Top 10. It does this by inspecting incoming HTTP/HTTPS traffic and applying a set of rules to detect and block malicious requests before they reach your backend servers. WAF can operate in two modes: detection mode, where it logs threats without blocking them, which is useful for initial testing and tuning; and prevention mode, where it actively blocks detected threats, which is the recommended mode for production environments. Implementing WAF centralizes your web application security, reducing the burden on individual backend servers and providing a consistent security posture across your application landscape. It's a powerful tool to safeguard your applications against a wide range of cyberattacks, ensuring data integrity and service availability. Web Application Firewall (WAF) means waf integrated with application gateway defends web applications against common exploits based on owasp rules, operating in detection or prevention mode.. In practical terms, protecting web applications from common vulnerabilities and exploits. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Azure Application Gateway's Layer 7 capabilities truly shine with features like URL-based routing and multi-site hosting. URL-based routing allows you to inspect the URL path of an incoming request and direct it to a specific backend pool. For example, if your application serves images from slash images slash asterisk and videos from slash video slash asterisk, you can configure the Application Gateway to send requests matching slash images slash asterisk to a backend pool optimized for image delivery, and slash video slash asterisk requests to a video streaming backend. This provides granular control over traffic distribution and allows for specialized backend services. Multi-site hosting takes this a step further by enabling you to host multiple distinct web applications on a single Application Gateway instance. It achieves this by examining the host header in the HTTP request. So, requests for site1. com can be routed to one set of backend servers, while requests for site2. com are sent to another, completely separate backend. This is incredibly cost-effective and simplifies management for organizations hosting multiple web properties. Both features leverage the Application Gateway's deep understanding of HTTP to provide flexible and efficient traffic management.

To effectively deploy and manage an Azure Application Gateway, it's essential to understand its core architectural components. First, we have the Frontend IP configuration, which is the public or private IP address where clients connect to the gateway. Next are Listeners, which define the IP address, port, and protocol—HTTP or HTTPS—for incoming client requests. Listeners are also responsible for handling SSL certificates for termination. Request routing rules are the heart of the gateway's intelligence; they link a listener to a backend pool and specify how requests matching the listener are routed, enabling URL-based routing and multi-site logic. Backend HTTP settings define parameters for how the Application Gateway connects to the backend servers, such as port, protocol, cookie-based affinity, and connection draining. Backend pools are groups of servers—VMs, VM scale sets, App Services, or external IPs—that host your web application. Finally, Health probes continuously monitor the health of these backend instances, ensuring traffic is only sent to healthy servers. These components work in concert to provide a robust and flexible web application delivery system. Application Gateway Components means application gateway's architecture comprises frontend ip, listeners, routing rules, http settings, backend pools, and health probes, all working together for intelligent traffic management.. Before you can deploy an Azure Application Gateway, it's crucial to understand its networking requirements, particularly regarding subnets. Application Gateway requires a dedicated subnet within your virtual network. This means that no other resources, such as virtual machines or other Azure services, should reside in the same subnet as your Application Gateway instances. This isolation ensures optimal performance and security for the gateway. The subnet size is also important; it must be large enough to accommodate the number of Application Gateway instances you plan to deploy, including any scaling needs. While there's no specific name requirement for this subnet, a slash 24 or slash 27 address prefix is commonly used, providing enough IP addresses for typical deployments. For example, a slash 27 subnet provides 32 IP addresses, of which 5 are reserved by Azure, leaving 27 usable IPs. This is usually sufficient for a standard Application Gateway deployment with scaling. Failing to provide a dedicated subnet or an adequately sized one is a common mistake that can lead to deployment failures or operational issues. Always plan your IP addressing carefully.

Now, let's begin the practical deployment of an Azure Application Gateway by setting up its foundational networking components. The first step involves creating a Public IP address. This public IP will serve as the external endpoint for your Application Gateway, allowing clients from the internet to reach your web applications. We'll use the Azure CLI to create a Standard SKU Public IP, ensuring it's static and zone-redundant for high availability. After creating the Application Gateway, the next critical step is to define its backend pool targets. A backend pool is essentially a collection of servers that host your web application. These can be virtual machines, virtual machine scale sets, Azure App Services, or even external IP addresses. As we conclude this chapter, let's recap the most important concepts related to Azure Application Gateway. First, remember that Application Gateway is a Layer 7 load balancer, meaning it understands HTTP and HTTPS traffic, enabling intelligent routing decisions based on URL paths or host headers. This is a key differentiator from Layer 4 load balancers. Second, Web Application Firewall, or WAF, is an integrated feature that provides crucial protection for your web applications against common vulnerabilities like S Q L injection and cross-site scripting, based on OWASP rule sets. It can operate in detection or prevention mode, offering flexibility in your security posture. Finally, SSL/TLS Termination, also known as SSL Offloading, is a powerful feature that decrypts incoming HTTPS traffic at the gateway, reducing the processing burden on your backend servers and simplifying their configuration. These three concepts form the bedrock of Application Gateway's value proposition, enabling secure, performant, and scalable web application delivery.

Let's continue our review of key concepts by focusing on Application Gateway's routing capabilities and architectural components. URL-based Routing allows you to direct traffic to different backend pools based on the specific URL path in the HTTP request, offering fine-grained control over where different parts of your application are served. Closely related is Multi-site Hosting, which enables a single Application Gateway instance to host multiple distinct web applications by using host headers to differentiate between domains. This is a highly efficient way to manage several web properties. From an architectural standpoint, a Listener defines the IP, port, and protocol for incoming client requests, acting as the entry point to the gateway. Request Routing Rules then link these listeners to backend pools, dictating the traffic flow. Finally, Backend Pools are the collections of servers that host your application, and Health Probes continuously monitor their availability. Understanding these elements is crucial for designing and implementing effective web application delivery solutions with Azure Application Gateway.
